title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 29–30
description: Advanced weather and climate terminology, figurative weather expressions, building and opportunity metaphors, register, idioms and nuanced collocations.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied published reference material for personal vocabulary study. Target expressions are selected from the reviewed teaching pages and exercises; Portuguese translations, usage notes and example sentences are independently written. Extended source passages, exercises and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Advanced Third Edition Units 29–30 teaching pages, A/B sections, illustrated prompts, exercises 29.1–29.5 and 30.1–30.5, and answer-key pages. Exercise-only scientific and building metaphors distinguished from teaching-page targets.
audit.pronunciation: Select broad British IPA for short words when confident; leave IPA blank for longer phrases or uncertain transcriptions. Word and sentence TTS targets were statically reviewed, not heard in a browser.
audit.languagePolicy: English in every field except natural Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Manual reading and cross-checking of unit teaching pages, notes, facing exercises and answer key; independently authored examples and explanations; structural and static audio-target checks performed programmatically. Browser import, actual TTS audio and recognition were not tested.
audit.limitations: No bundled MP3 recordings. Static checks do not establish working in-browser import, voice pronunciation or speech recognition. Weather slang and building idioms vary by region and register.

units.title: Unit 29 — Weather and climate
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 29. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Natural world and figurative language · weather, climate and metaphor
learningObjectives: Use near-synonyms with appropriate informal and neutral registers when discussing temperature, wind, rainfall and humidity.
Understand how climate, clouds, sunshine, snow, hail, thunder and wind are used metaphorically in evaluations and reports.
Select natural metaphorical collocations such as a frosty reception, a hail of abuse and snowed under with work.
Explain climate-science terminology such as mean temperature, precipitation, latitude and seasonality.

sectionsChecked: A · Weather conversations, near-synonyms and levels of formality
B · Climate metaphors, figurative collocations and contrasting forms
Exercises 29.1–29.4, technical climate passage and answer-key entries

items.pt: frio; fresquinho, especialmente de maneira desconfortável
items.example: It was chilly enough to wear a jacket on the evening walk.
items.note: A common, mild-to-moderate description of cold weather.

items.example: We were freezing after waiting an hour in the wind.
items.note: Informal intensifier for very cold conditions; not necessarily literally below zero.

items.example: The morning was rather nippy, despite the clear sky.
items.note: Informal British English for noticeably cold weather.

items.example: It was boiling in the lecture hall without air conditioning.
items.note: Informal figurative description of extreme heat.

items.example: The workers had to endure sweltering conditions in the warehouse.
items.note: Strong adjective for unpleasantly hot weather or environments.

items.example: We were roasting on the crowded bus in midsummer.
items.note: Informal and expressive description of feeling very hot.

items.example: It was too blowy for the children to play badminton outside.
items.note: Informal, especially British, describing a windy day.

items.example: It was a bright but breezy afternoon by the harbour.
items.note: Often implies a pleasant or moderate wind, unlike strong gales.

items.example: The oppressive afternoon heat made working outdoors exhausting.
items.note: Describes heavy, uncomfortable heat; also figuratively oppressive conditions or regimes.

items.example: The garden was still warm on the sultry summer evening.
items.note: Suggests uncomfortable heat and humidity; can have other figurative uses.

items.example: The stifling air in the room made it hard to concentrate.
items.note: Stronger than warm, suggesting a lack of fresh air.

items.example: The heavy air before the storm made everyone feel tired.
items.note: Here heavy describes oppressive atmospheric conditions, not the literal weight of air.

items.example: The air felt close and uncomfortable in the crowded room.
items.note: Close pronounced /kləʊs/ means stuffy or airless in this weather sense.

items.example: A sudden downpour forced the guests to seek shelter.
items.note: A heavy, intense fall of rain; countable noun.

items.example: After the deluge, several streets were under water.
items.note: Often more dramatic or literary than downpour; also figurative a flood of something.

items.example: We stayed inside because it was chucking it down outside.
items.note: Very informal British idiom for raining heavily; the spoken target is a complete short clause.

items.pt: está chovendo muito; está caindo um toró
items.example: Take an umbrella because it is pouring at the moment.
items.note: Everyday expression for heavy rain; the literal verb pour also means make a liquid flow.

items.pt: úmido; com alta umidade do ar
items.example: The coastal air remains humid even after sunset.
items.note: Neutral description of high moisture in the air.

items.example: The muggy afternoon made the short walk exhausting.
items.note: Informal and usually unpleasantly warm and humid.

items.pt: úmido e pegajoso; frio e suado
items.example: The room felt clammy after several days of rain.
items.note: Often used of unpleasant damp conditions or of skin that is damp and cool.

items.pt: tempo quente e úmido; clima pegajoso
items.example: Sticky weather makes commuting uncomfortable in crowded trains.
items.note: Figurative description of hot, humid conditions; sticky literally refers to adhering surfaces.

items.example: Repeated secrecy created a climate of distrust within the organisation.
items.note: Climate describes an overall social atmosphere, not literal weather.

items.pt: clima de mudança; ambiente favorável a mudanças
items.example: A climate of change emerged after the new management team arrived.
items.note: Metaphorical use of climate for prevailing circumstances.

items.example: The economic climate made investors more cautious about expansion.
items.note: A strongly established collocation; not the same as meteorological climate.

items.example: The political climate has made long-term negotiations more difficult.
items.note: Refers to prevailing political attitudes and circumstances.

items.example: The social climate became more tolerant following the reforms.
items.note: Metaphorical climate meaning the overall social atmosphere.

items.example: The prevailing climate discouraged employees from questioning decisions.
items.note: Prevailing means dominant at a particular time; also collocates with winds and opinion.

items.example: Her sunny disposition helped calm the team during the crisis.
items.note: Figurative sunny means consistently positive or cheerful.

items.example: Despite the setbacks, the director kept a sunny outlook on the project.
items.note: Sunny can suggest optimism about the future, not just fine weather.

items.example: The proposed cuts received a frosty reception from staff.
items.note: Frosty suggests an unfriendly or unwelcoming response.

items.example: I am snowed under with work until the final report is submitted.
items.note: Informal phrase meaning having more tasks than one can comfortably manage.

items.pt: sob suspeita; com a reputação abalada
items.example: The manager left the company under a cloud following the inquiry.
items.note: Metaphor indicating suspicion or disapproval, rather than a physical cloud.

items.pt: prejudicar seu discernimento; turvar seu julgamento
items.example: Do not let personal loyalty cloud your judgement of the evidence.
items.note: A cloud can obscure clear reasoning; British spelling judgement.

items.pt: rajada de balas; saraivada de tiros
items.example: The convoy was met with a hail of bullets at the checkpoint.
items.note: Hail metaphorically suggests a large, rapid succession of projectiles.

items.pt: enxurrada de insultos; torrente de ofensas
items.example: The decision provoked a hail of abuse online.
items.note: A fixed metaphorical phrase for numerous hostile remarks.

items.pt: tempestade de críticas ofensivas; enxurrada de insultos
items.example: The referee faced a storm of abuse after the controversial match.
items.note: Highlights the scale and intensity of verbal hostility.

items.example: I have only a hazy memory of the first workshop.
items.note: Hazy implies indistinct, unclear recollection.

items.pt: brumas da história; passado remoto e nebuloso
items.example: The settlement’s origins are lost in the mists of history.
items.note: Literary expression for the remote, poorly documented past.

items.example: The sudden announcement caused a whirlwind of speculation in the press.
items.note: Whirlwind represents rapid, intense activity or reactions.

items.example: Their whirlwind romance led to a wedding within two months.
items.note: Strong collocation meaning a passionate relationship that develops very quickly.

items.pt: passar estrondosamente; avançar fazendo grande barulho
items.example: Heavy lorries thundered down the narrow street before dawn.
items.note: Figurative movement accompanied by loud, deep noise.

items.example: The performance ended to thunderous applause from the audience.
items.note: Thunderous concerns loud noise, contrasting with thundery for stormy weather.

items.pt: tempo de trovoada; tempo com ameaça de temporal
items.example: The forecast warned of thundery weather in the afternoon.
items.note: Use thundery for weather involving or suggesting thunder; thunderous is usually for sound.

items.example: The winds of change were evident across the industry.
items.note: Conventional metaphor for emerging changes in society or an organisation.

items.pt: ventos de insatisfação; sinais de descontentamento crescente
items.example: The winds of discontent spread after the wage negotiations failed.
items.note: A metaphorical extension indicating the spread of dissatisfaction.

items.example: The mean annual temperature has risen over the recorded period.
items.note: Mean is the arithmetic average in this scientific context.

items.pt: precipitação; chuva, neve e outras formas de água que caem da atmosfera
items.example: The region receives most of its precipitation in winter.
items.note: Technical collective term for rain, snow and similar water falling from clouds.

items.example: Researchers compared rainfall seasonality across several regions.
items.note: Changes or patterns associated with seasons of the year.

items.pt: latitude; distância angular em relação ao Equador
items.example: Latitude influences the amount of daylight received during the year.
items.note: Geographic position north or south of the Equator, measured in degrees.

items.example: Solar radiation affects the energy balance at the Earth’s surface.
items.note: Energy arriving from the Sun in the form of electromagnetic radiation.

items.pt: elevação; altitude acima do nível do mar
items.example: At higher elevation, average temperatures are often lower.
items.note: In this climate context, height above sea level.

items.example: Few crops survive without irrigation in the arid valley.
items.note: Dry climatic conditions with very little rainfall.

items.pt: clima continental; típico de regiões distantes do oceano
items.example: The inland town experiences a continental climate with cold winters.
items.note: Inland climatic conditions generally less moderated by nearby seas.

items.pt: amenizar as temperaturas; reduzir seus extremos
items.example: Proximity to the sea can moderate temperatures throughout the year.
items.note: The verb moderate means make less extreme, not simply average the measurements.

units.title: Unit 30 — Brick walls and glass ceilings
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 30. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Metaphorical language · buildings, barriers, opportunities and success
learningObjectives: Interpret figurative meanings of building parts such as wall, roof, ceiling, tower, window, door and key.
Use fixed idioms for limits, barriers and opportunities with accurate verbs and prepositions.
Distinguish a glass ceiling, an ivory tower, a brick wall and a tower of strength.
Recognise additional exercise-based metaphors about hardship, silence, foundations and personal responsibility.

sectionsChecked: A · Building metaphors, idioms, emotional reactions and restrictions
B · Entrances, opportunity metaphors and key collocations

items.pt: elogiar excessivamente alguém; criar grandes expectativas sobre alguém
items.example: The media built the young scientist up as the next great innovator.
items.note: Separable phrasal verb here meaning raise expectations by praising; it may create pressure.

items.pt: consolidar uma parceria; fortalecer uma relação
items.example: The joint research project helped cement a partnership between the universities.
items.note: Cement metaphorically makes a relationship more secure or durable.

items.word: come up against a brick wall
items.example: Every request for the records seemed to come up against a brick wall.
items.note: Fixed idiom for encountering a strong obstacle; often figurative bureaucracy or resistance.

items.example: The contract imposes a ceiling on spending for the first year.
items.note: Ceiling is a maximum limit, not literally the top of a room.

items.pt: teto de vidro; barreira invisível ao crescimento profissional
items.example: Several employees described a glass ceiling blocking promotion to senior posts.
items.note: An invisible career barrier, especially for women and other underrepresented groups.

items.word: the roof fell in on my world
items.example: When I heard the sudden news, the roof fell in on my world.
items.note: Strong metaphor for a devastating personal event; wording adapts to the speaker.

items.pt: o chão pareceu desaparecer; senti que ia desmaiar
items.example: When she stood up too quickly, she felt as though the floor gave way.
items.note: The unit notes the floor giving way figuratively in relation to fainting; also literal collapse.

items.example: Housing costs have gone through the roof in the city centre.
items.note: Informal idiom for a rapid, substantial increase, particularly prices.

items.example: The manager hit the roof when the confidential report was leaked.
items.note: Informal: become extremely angry, not a price increase.

items.example: The company has a narrow window of opportunity to secure the grant.
items.note: A limited period in which a favourable action is possible.

items.pt: ir por água abaixo; desaparecer completamente
items.example: All our plans went out of the window when the funding was withdrawn.
items.note: Figurative loss or abandonment of a quality, plan or expectation.

items.pt: torre de marfim; isolamento da realidade
items.example: The researcher was accused of living in an ivory tower.
items.note: Disapproving image of intellectual detachment from ordinary practical realities.

items.pt: pilar de apoio; pessoa que dá enorme suporte emocional
items.example: Her closest friend was a tower of strength during the recovery.
items.note: A person who provides dependable emotional rather than physical strength.

items.example: Her research record towers above those of many competitors.
items.note: Can describe remarkable height or figurative superiority.

items.pt: porta de entrada para uma carreira
items.example: The internship proved a gateway to a career in data science.
items.note: Gateway to signals a route or opportunity leading to something.

items.example: Speaking another language can open doors in international research.
items.note: Figurative expression for making opportunities accessible.

items.example: A poor decision early on can close doors later in a career.
items.note: Figurative opposite of open doors; often used with plural doors.

items.word: close the door on the past
items.pt: deixar o passado para trás; encerrar uma fase
items.example: After resigning, she wanted to close the door on the past and start again.
items.note: Idiom for decisively leaving a period or experience behind.

items.pt: pelos fundos; por meios informais ou não oficiais
items.example: The rule was introduced by the back door without public consultation.
items.note: Figurative means a route that bypasses normal official procedures.

items.example: The final negotiations took place behind closed doors.
items.note: Used when events happen privately and details are withheld from the public.

items.pt: fornecer a chave para; oferecer a solução para
items.example: The experiment may provide the key to understanding the failure.
items.note: Conventional metaphor for something that makes a solution possible.

items.pt: ter a chave para; ser decisivo para
items.example: Accurate measurements may hold the key to solving the problem.
items.note: Means possess or constitute the crucial factor needed for success.

items.example: Consistent practice was the key to success in the training programme.
items.note: Fixed nominal pattern: the key to followed by noun or -ing form.

items.example: Choosing the test strategy is a key decision for the project.
items.note: Key as an adjective means essential or especially important.

items.word: keep the wolf from the door
items.pt: ganhar apenas o suficiente para sobreviver; afastar a miséria
items.example: She took temporary jobs to keep the wolf from the door while looking for work.
items.note: Fixed idiom meaning avoid poverty or hunger, often with barely or just enough.

items.pt: muro de silêncio; silêncio absoluto e coletivo
items.example: The investigator encountered a wall of silence among the witnesses.
items.note: Metaphor for a complete or deliberate lack of response.

items.pt: lançar as bases para; estabelecer os fundamentos de
items.example: The pilot study helped lay the foundations for a larger investigation.
items.note: Common metaphor for putting in place what future progress will depend on.

items.example: After the prolonged dispute, their business lay in ruins.
items.note: Can describe literal destroyed structures or figurative collapse of plans and organisations.

items.pt: arrumar a própria casa; resolver os próprios problemas antes de criticar outros
items.example: The director was told to clean up his own backyard before advising other teams.
items.note: Idiom highlighting hypocrisy when criticising others while neglecting local problems; more common in US contexts.
